en: The Sūtra on the Miscellaneous Collection Spoken by the Buddha,
translated by the Śramaṇa Faxian of Pingyang during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.
Among the disciples of the Buddha, the various Arhats each excel in their respective practices, just as Śāriputra does.
Śāriputra was foremost in wisdom and delighted in expounding the subtle and wondrous Dharma;

Maudgalyāyana was foremost in supernormal powers, constantly traveling by means of his spiritual penetrations to the six realms of existence to witness sentient beings receiving the retributions of their good and evil deeds, and returning to speak of them for the sake of humans.

On another occasion, Maudgalyāyana went to the banks of the Ganges and saw a multitude of five hundred hungry ghosts approaching the water; there was a water-guarding ghost who, wielding an iron staff, drove them away so that they could not draw near.
Thereupon, the various hungry ghosts went directly to where Maudgalyāyana was, prostrated at his feet, and each asked about the causes and conditions for their offenses.
One ghost said to Maudgalyāyana:
"Virtuous One!..."

Having received this body, I have constantly suffered from heat and thirst; hearing previously that these waters of the Ganges were cool and sweet, I joyfully approached them and entered them to bathe, but they immediately became boiling hot, and my entire body was scorched and ruined.
"If one drinks even a single mouthful, the five viscera are scorched and rotted, and the stench is unbearable.
By what causes and conditions does one undergo such retribution?
Maudgalyāyana replied:

“In a previous life, you were an interpreter of physiognomy who assessed the fortune and misfortune of others; your words were mostly false with little truth, and you would either disparage or praise them.
You claimed to be discerning and profound in order to stir the hearts of men;
through deceit, delusion, and fraud, you sought after gain and offerings.”
Deluded sentient beings lose what they desire.
Therefore, although they hear today that this water is cool and delicious, upon reaching it, it does not meet their expectations.
This is the "flower-retribution" for their evil deeds; only later will they undergo the bitter retribution of hell.
Again, another ghost said to Maudgalyāyana:

"I am constantly devoured by large dogs with sharp teeth and red eyes who eat my flesh until only bones remain; the wind then blows them up again, my flesh grows back, and the dogs come once more to devour me."
"I constantly undergo this suffering; for what cause and condition does it happen?
Maudgalyāyana replied, "In a previous life, you were the master of a celestial shrine.
You constantly instructed sentient beings to slaughter sheep to offer their blood to the gods, while you yourself ate the meat. For this reason, today you must repay them with flesh."
"This is merely the preliminary flowering of their evil conduct; later they shall undergo the bitter fruit of hell, a hundred thousand times ten million times greater.
Again, another ghost addressed Maudgalyāyana, saying:
"Virtuous One!..."
"My body is constantly covered all over with excrement, which I also eat.
For what cause and condition do I undergo such suffering?
Maudgalyāyana said to him:
"In a previous life, you were a Brahmin who was wicked, perverse, and did not believe in the retribution of sin and merit.
When there was a mendicant monk, you intended not to let him come again."
He immediately took that bowl, filled it to the brim with excrement, placed some rice on top, and brought it to the practitioner.
Having received it, the practitioner carried it back to his original place;
as he ate the rice with his hand, the excrement defiled his hand.
"Therefore, today we undergo such retribution.
This is the 'flower-like' preliminary reward for our evil conduct; only later shall we suffer the bitter fruit of hell.
Then another ghost addressed Maudgalyāyana, saying:
“Venerable Sir!
My belly is as vast as a jar, yet my throat, hands, and feet are as thin as needles; thus I am unable to obtain food or drink.
For what cause and condition do I undergo such suffering?”
Maudgalyāyana replied:
“In a previous life, you were the head of a village. Relying on your own wealth and nobility, you drank wine and acted wantonly;
you treated others with contempt and deceit, seizing their food and drink and leaving sentient beings hungry and distressed. Due to these causes and conditions, you have undergone such punishment.”
"This is merely the preliminary retribution; the bitter fruits of hell await you yet.
Furthermore, another ghost said to Maudgalyāyana:
"I constantly go to latrines, desiring to eat excrement."
There is a great multitude of ghosts who, seizing staffs, drive me away so that I may not approach the latrine.
My mouth is festering and foul-smelling; I am hungry, exhausted, and destitute.
By what causes and conditions do I undergo such suffering?
Maudgalyāyana replied:
"In a previous life, you were the superintendent of a Buddhist monastery (vihārasvāmin). There were several lay practitioners who made offerings to the Saṃgha, providing them with food and utensils."
If visiting monks come, you provide them with coarse offerings;
once the visiting monks have departed, you eat the fine food yourself.
Because of this cause and condition, it is difficult even to obtain excrement, let alone good food.
"This is merely the preliminary retribution; later, you shall undergo the fruits of hell.
Again, another ghost said to Maudgalyāyana:
"My body is entirely covered with tongues; axes come to hack at my tongues, which are severed and then grow back again, continuing in this manner without end."
"For what reason did this happen?
Maudgalyāyana replied, "In a previous life, you were a practitioner of the Way.

When the community of monks appointed you to prepare honey syrup, the blocks of rock honey were too large to dissolve easily, so you used an axe to chop them. Then, with a mind of theft, you ate a single mouthful."
"For this reason, the axe returns and cuts my tongue.
Furthermore, another ghost said to Maudgalyāyana:
"I always have seven red-hot iron balls that enter my mouth directly; they pass into my belly and scorch and rot my five internal organs, then emerge only to enter again."
"For what cause and condition did you receive such punishment?
Maudgalyāyana replied, "In a previous life, you were a śrāmaṇera.

While gathering melon seeds, you went to your teacher; out of respect for him, you showed partiality by giving him seven more than there actually were. For this reason, you have received such punishment."
"This is but the preliminary retribution; later, you shall undergo the fruit of hell.
Again, another ghost said to Maudgalyāyana:
"There are always two hot iron wheels revolving beneath both my armpits, and my body is scorched and putrefied."
"For what reason is this so?

Maudgalyāyana replied, "In a previous life, while you were making cakes for the community of monks, you took two portions with a thieving mind, tucking them under both your armpits; therefore, you have received such retribution."
"This is merely the flower-retribution; only later will you suffer the fruit of hell.
Furthermore, another hungry ghost said to Maudgalyāyana:
"My ball is as large as a jar; when walking, I carry it on my shoulder, and when standing, I sit upon it. My every movement is plagued by suffering."
"For what reason is it thus?
Maudgalyāyana replied, "In a previous life, you served as a market official.

You constantly gave with light weights and small measures, but took with heavy weights and large measures. Always desiring great profit for yourself, you oppressed and exploited others; therefore, you have received such retribution."
"This is merely the preliminary retribution; the bitter fruits of hell await you yet.
Furthermore, another ghost addressed Maudgalyāyana, saying:
"I always have eyes upon my two shoulders and a mouth and nose upon my chest, yet I never possess a head."
"For what reason is it so?
Maudgalyāyana replied, "In a previous life,
you were constantly the apprentice of an executioner."
"When you were killing criminals, you always felt a heart of joy as you bound their hair with ropes and pulled them; for this reason, you have come to suffer such retribution."
"This is but the preliminary flowering of my evil deeds; the bitter fruit of hell awaits me yet.
Furthermore, another ghost addressed Maudgalyāyana, saying:
"Constantly there are hot iron needles entering and exiting my body, and I suffer this misery beyond all endurance."
"For what reason is it thus?
Maudgalyāyana replied, "In your previous life,
you were a trainer of horses, or perhaps a trainer of elephants."
"Elephants and horses are difficult to restrain; you pierced their feet with iron needles.
At other times, when oxen were slow, you likewise pierced them with needles. For this reason, you undergo such punishment.
This is but the flower-like retribution for your evil deeds; the bitter fruits of hell await you yet."
Again, another ghost said to Maudgalyāyana:
"Fire constantly issues from my body, burning me with intense heat and distress.
By what causes and conditions does this occur?"
Maudgalyāyana replied:
"In a previous life, you were the queen of a king. There was another queen whom the king greatly favored; you constantly harbored jealousy toward her and sought opportunities to harm her."

While the king was away from his bed after rising, his beloved queen was still asleep and had not yet put on her clothes. He immediately conceived an evil intent; finding that he was just then making cakes containing hot sesame oil, he poured it over her abdomen. Her abdomen was burned and she died instantly.
"By these causes and conditions, I undergo such punishment.
Furthermore, another ghost said to Maudgalyāyana:
"A whirlwind constantly turns my body around; I have no autonomy to go east or west as I please, and my mind is perpetually distressed and oppressed."
"For what cause and condition did this happen?
Maudgalyāyana replied, "In a previous life, you were constantly a diviner;

sometimes you spoke the truth, and sometimes you spoke falsehoods, thereby deluding people's minds so that they could not act according to their own will. For this reason, you have received such retribution."
"This is merely the preliminary retribution; the bitter fruits of hell await you later.
Again, another ghost addressed Maudgalyāyana, saying:
"My body is always like a lump of flesh, devoid of hands, feet, eyes, ears, nose, and so forth. I am constantly devoured by insects and birds, and my suffering from this transgression is unbearable."
"For what reason is this so?
Maudgalyāyana replied, "In a previous life, you constantly gave others medicine that caused them to miscarry their children; for this reason, you have received such retribution."
"This is merely the preliminary retribution; the bitter fruits of hell await us yet.
Furthermore, another ghost addressed Maudgalyāyana, saying:
"Constantly there is a hot iron cage that falls upon my body, scorching and tormenting me with distress."
"For what cause and condition do you undergo such suffering?
Maudgalyāyana replied, "In a previous life, you constantly used nets to capture fish and birds; for this reason, you undergo such suffering."
"This is the preliminary flowering of my evil conduct; the bitter fruit shall follow later.
Again, another ghost addressed Maudgalyāyana, saying:
"I cover my head with a cloth to conceal it, yet I am also constantly afraid that someone will come to kill me. My mind is perpetually terrified and filled with dread, which I cannot endure."
"For what reason is this so?
Maudgalyāyana replied, "In a previous life, you committed adultery with another's wife.

You were constantly afraid of being seen by others, fearing that her husband might capture, bind, and beat you to death, or fearing that the law of the state might execute you in the marketplace. Because you harbored such continuous terror, you have received this retribution."
"This is merely the preliminary flowering of their evil deeds; they shall later undergo the actual fruit of hell. Again, another ghost asked:

"I have received this body, upon whose shoulders there is always a copper vessel filled with molten copper. Holding a ladle in my hand, I take it from the vessel and pour it over my head; my entire body is scorched and ruined. I suffer in this manner, countless and immeasurable times."
"For what cause and condition has your transgression become such as this?

Maudgalyāyana replied, "In a previous life, when you had left the household life to pursue the Way, you were in charge of the Sangha's food and drink; you took a jar of ghee and secretly placed it elsewhere."
When a visiting practitioner arrived, [the resident] did not give him any; once he had departed, [the resident] took out some ghee and distributed it to the resident monks.
This ghee was the property of the *caitya* Sangha, to which all have an equal share.
"This person concealed [the truth], and thus, although it was not equal to [others],
for this reason they undergo this retribution.
Maudgalyāyana further saw a celestial maiden sitting upon a lotus flower one hundred yojanas in length and breadth.

This flower alone is exquisite, surpassing all others; whatever requisites for life one desires—whether palaces, halls, food, or drink—all emerge from the flower according to one's thoughts, following one wherever one goes.
Maudgalyāyana asked,
"What wholesome deeds did you perform to receive such a retribution?
The goddess replied:
"After the parinirvāṇa of Kāśyapa Buddha, his entire relics were left behind.
His disciples constructed a stūpa made of the seven precious gems, forty *li* in height and breadth.

At that time, I was born as a woman; upon seeing the marks and signs of the Buddha’s image within the precious stūpa, a feeling of faith and reverence arose in me. Recalling the merits of the Buddha, I removed the flowers from my head and offered them to the image."
"It is because of these causes and conditions that the retribution he receives is uniquely sublime in this way.
At a time of intense summer heat, Śāriputra was traveling and arrived at the Āmra Grove.
There was a laborer who was drawing well water to irrigate the trees.
This man had no great faith in the Buddha, but upon seeing Śāriputra, he conceived a small measure of faith and called out to him, saying,
"Venerable One!..."
"Come, let us sit beneath this tree to remove our garments; I shall sprinkle you with water so that you may receive irrigation without loss, and moreover, we shall both benefit one another.
Thereupon, Śāriputra removed his robes and received the wash; his body attained coolness and comfort, and he wandered about as he pleased.
That laborer passed away that very night and was reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, possessing great majesty and power.
Next, Śakra Devānām Indra thought to himself:
"By what cause have I been born here?"
He reflected upon his own past lives and saw that his faith had been slight; it was because he had worked as a laborer irrigating fields that he calculated the water for bathing Śāriputra.
"If my faith had been pure and profound, I would have known there must be a karmic reward; therefore, I prepared these bathing implements as an act of offering."
"Reflecting upon myself, although my merit was slight, because I encountered this fertile field [of virtue], the reward obtained is truly great!
He then went to where Śāriputra was and scattered flowers as an offering.
Śāriputra, moved by his heart of pure faith, immediately preached the Dharma for him, and he attained the stage of Srotāpanna.
Maudgalyāyana, in turn, saw another spirit whose body was immense and who possessed golden hands; from the five fingers of these hands, nectar constantly flowed.
Whatever travelers required—be it food, drink, or necessities of life—all emerged from the fingers, which the spirit bestowed upon them as they desired.
Maudgalyāyana asked,
"Which deva are you?
Your karmic rewards and meritorious virtues are so extraordinary!"
The celestial king replied:
"I am not the King of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, nor even the King of the sixth heaven, nor am I the Brahmā King.
I am a great spirit who dwells in a great city within that kingdom; I have come here for the purpose of traveling about and sightseeing."
Maudgalyāyana asked,
"What wholesome deeds did you perform to obtain such a reward?
He replied:
"In that country there is a great city named Rauruka.
In the past, I lived within it as a poor woman, weaving woolen bags and selling them to support myself."

As his livelihood grew increasingly impoverished and his house fell completely into ruin, he eventually went out to the street and lived by weaving bags near the home of a wealthy elder who was fond of practicing charity.
When the sun was about to reach its zenith, if there were śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who, carrying their alms bowls, went begging for food and asked me:
"Where is the house of such-and-such a householder?"
"My heart is true and free from falsehood; with joy, I raise my hand and point toward his house, saying: 'Go there! Go there!'"
"The time is nearly past; do not seek further.
For this reason, she has received such a reward.
If even a poor woman who rejoiced in the merit of another’s act of giving receives such a reward as this, how much more so for one who actually practices giving?
During the time when the Buddha was in the world, there were five great kings.
During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, they had been spiritual friends who left the household life to practice the Way.
When Śākyamuni Buddha appeared in the world, they all attained the fruit of the Path.
I shall now relate the causes and conditions by which a certain king attained the Way.
There was a kingdom named Paṇḍitī, and its king was named Udrana. That country was prosperous and wealthy, and its population was flourishing.
The king had twenty thousand consorts; his first consort was named Candraprabhā (Moonlight), whose appearance and demeanor were upright and graceful, and whom the king deeply cherished and respected.
On one occasion, when the king held a great assembly and performed various musical entertainments, he commanded Candraprabhā to dance.

Lady Candraprabhā was dressed in upper garments and adorned her body with gold, silver, and famous jewels, as well as necklaces; she danced with such extraordinary grace that she delighted the hearts of the assembly.

The King, being skilled in physiognomy, perceived signs appearing on his lady that indicated her end would come within half a year; she then suddenly passed away. Stricken by the suffering of separation from his beloved, he was so overwhelmed by grief that he could not look upon her.

Candraprabha was astonished and questioned him about it. Because the matter of his death was so grave, the King feared that Candraprabha would become distressed; thus, he concealed the truth and did not speak of it.
When Candraprabha pressed him with repeated inquiries, the King finally replied:
"Your lifespan is short and you will soon come to your end. It is because of the pain of being separated from those you love that I am grieving."
Candraprabha said:
"Now, that birth is followed by death is the constant law of the world; why should you alone be so sorrowful?
If you have such great affection for me, simply inform me, and allow me to leave the household life."
The king approved of these words and permitted him to enter the Path.
Desiring to verify the retribution of karmic results and to strengthen his faith, the king made a solemn vow with him, saying:
"If you leave the household life, uphold the precepts, and practice contemplation, even if you do not achieve the Way, you will certainly be reborn in the heavens."
"Once you have been reborn in the heavens, return to my place;
I will grant you permission to leave the household life.
Candraprabha immediately consented to this vow.
Thereupon, she summoned the bhikṣuṇīs and immediately ordained her, taking her away.

Because she was of noble status and had been able to renounce the five desires, many people came to inquire after her, pay their respects, and offer her sustenance; these things hindered her spiritual practice, and for this reason she traveled through various kingdoms.

From the day he left the household life, after a full six months had passed, he maintained the precepts with purity, diligently contemplated the Path, grew weary of the world, and attained the stage of Anāgāmin.
Having passed away from that village, he was immediately reborn in the Heaven of Form.
Reflecting upon his past causes and conditions, he realized he had a significant obligation to the king and felt compelled to fulfill his original vow.
He observed that the king was submerged in the five desires and was stubborn, difficult to transform.
If one were to approach him directly, there would be no way to move him; it is appropriate to use intimidation, for only then will he submit.

He then transformed himself into a great rākṣasa, his body hair bristling, and wielding a five-foot sword. Taking advantage of the king’s quiet sleep at night, he remained in the air not far from him.
When the king awoke, he was filled with great terror and said:
"Though you possess tens of millions of troops, they now belong solely to me; you have no autonomy."
"The time of my death has arrived; by what means can I be saved?
The king replied, "I have no other means;
I rely solely upon the merit of past good deeds and the purity of my cultivated mind, so that at death I shall be reborn in a favorable realm."
The deity agreed with these words, saying:
"By such causes and conditions, this is the most reliable;
there is no other principle! The king then asked:
“Who are you, O deity, that causes me such great fear and makes me shrink back?
The deva replied:
“I am Queen Candraprabhā. Having been permitted by the King to leave the household life, I contemplated the transcendence of desire and was reborn in the Heaven of Form.”
"I have now come to meet you at this crucial juncture.
The King said, "Though you speak thus, I still do not believe you. Only when you restore yourself to your original form will I believe you."
The deva immediately transformed his appearance to resemble Candraprabha, with his robes and ornaments as they were before, and stood beside the king.
As desire arose in the king, he moved forward, intending to seize him.
Candraprabha thought to himself, "This person’s desires and state are impure; how can I draw near him?
Thereupon, he immediately returned and ascended into the void.
He preached the Dharma for the king, saying to him:
"This body is impermanent; it cannot be preserved for even the snap of a finger. It is like the morning dew, which vanishes as soon as the sun rises.
Not only is it impermanent, but you are greedily attached to this body—do you not see this, O King?"

The flourishing bloom of youth is swallowed up and destroyed by old age; the faculties decay and fail, the eyesight grows dim and the hearing dull; the physical form collapses into putrefaction, no longer possessing any value.

It is like brewing wine: once the pure essence has been extracted, the dregs have no value. So too, this body, having grown old, possesses nothing worth craving or delighting in; there is only death remaining.
Once this body has been born, death is ever its companion; do you not see it?

There are those who die in the womb, those who die upon leaving the womb, those who die in their prime, and those who die in old age. This body is precarious and fragile; the thief of death constantly follows it, and it cannot be relied upon for even a moment.

The body and mind are ablaze with fire, consisting solely of manifold sufferings; the mind harbors the three poisons and afflictions, while the body endures various ailments such as cold, heat, hunger, and thirst—yet one feels no revulsion, remaining greedily attached to this self-body.

The palace attendants and courtesans, the splendors of the five desires, the state’s wealth, and one's wife and children—all these are not mine; when death arrives, not a single thing follows along. If even the body itself is abandoned, how much more so other things?

Birth and death, sorrow and joy—none of these are worth marveling at. Ordinary, petty, and ignorant beings, shrouded in darkness, are deluded and submerged within the five desires; they wander through the cycle of birth and death, knowing no way out.
"The King is a man of wisdom; why does he not feel weary of the world and leave the household life to seek the Way?
At that time, a wholesome mind arose in the King, and he granted his permission for him to leave the household life.
Candraprabha exhorted him once more, saying:

"If you should go forth into homelessness, you must seek a good teacher and hear the sublime Dharma; having heard the sublime Dharma, you must receive it and practice it, exerting yourselves with diligence day and night, remaining alert and tireless!"
Having spoken these words, he suddenly vanished.
When dawn broke, the king abdicated the throne to his crown prince, renounced the five desires, and went to Kātyāyana to leave the household life and pursue the Way.

At that time, because the king had renounced heavy worldly honors and sought the true and correct Way, many ministers, officials, and common people came to offer him sustenance, paying him their respects and inquiring after his well-being.
Fearing that it would hinder his cultivation of the path, he traveled on until he reached the kingdom of Magadha. The Buddha preached the Dharma for him, and he attained the stage of Arhat.

With his faculties stilled and silent, free from all desire, he took up a clay alms-bowl and entered the city of Rājagṛha. Having obtained leftover rice through alms-gathering, he returned to the forest at noon, sat upon the grass, and ate.
King Bimbisāra encountered him while out on a journey; he went to the forest to inquire after him, saying:

"In the past, you were a king, with a retinue escorting you in and out as you struck bells and beat drums; the villages and settlements, the revenues and treasuries, and all manner of rare treasures and means of livelihood were naturally at your disposal."
"Now you have become a beggar, wandering alone to beg for food; how could this be a joy?
You should return home and give up the path; let us rule half the kingdom together!
The practitioner replied:
"I am a great king with many settlements.
For what reason now would I abandon the great for the small?
This is not fitting for me!"
King Bimbisāra asked again:
"In the past, you ate the finest delicacies served in precious vessels; now, holding an earthen bowl and begging for leftover food from the previous night—is this not difficult?"
Formerly you were a king, attended by brave warriors and soldiers; today you are alone—how can you not feel terror?

Formerly you dwelt in the deep palace, entertained by ladies, consorts, and court dancers, with exquisite sounds and beautiful sights filling your ears and eyes; you sat upon jeweled couches spread with fine silken rugs and soft mattresses.
Today you drift away, sleeping alone in the forests and wilds upon a bed of straw—how bitter it must be!
The practitioner replied, "I am content with this;
I have no craving or delight for anything.
King Bimbisāra said:
"You are a pitiable person!
The practitioner replied,
"You are the pitiable person, not I!"
Why is this? You are entangled by the five desires and driven by affection, unable to attain self-mastery.
My mind is now tranquil and joyful; free from desire and at ease, I experience manifold happiness.
After he had preached the Dharma for King Bimbisāra, the king immediately departed.
He asked:

"These four assemblies all love the Buddha-way and wish to practice the three matters of a bodhisattva. Some wish to practice for one day and one night, some wish to practice for seven days, and there are even those who wish to practice for their entire lives. How much merit will they obtain?"
He replied: "This question is extremely profound; I am unable to answer it. Only the Buddha can know the measure of this merit.
Apart from the Tathāgata, no one can comprehend it!"
For instance, when the King of the Yuezhi sought the Buddha-way, he constructed thirty-two stupas to make offerings to the marks of the Buddha.
While constructing them one by one, upon reaching the thirty-first, an evil person offended the king, causing his mind to regress:
"How can such an evil person be saved?"
Immediately, he turned his mind away from birth and death toward Nirvana and constructed the thirty-second stupa to seek liberation.
By virtue of these causes and conditions, he attained the path of an Arhat; therefore, this monastery is named Pratimokṣa, which in the language of Qin means "liberation from birth and death."
"From that time until now, less than two hundred years have passed; this monastery still exists today, and I have seen it myself. In every temple there are fine images.
After the King had passed away, a person obtained a flower from an *āmra* tree, its color like gold.
This person obtains beautiful flowers and wishes to make them into head ornaments, but then reflects to himself:
"This head is impermanent; when it perishes, it will be devoured by foxes and dogs and flow away as one with dung and soil—what use is there in adorning it?"
He immediately took it into the Buddha stupa and, seeing the marks and signs of the Buddha’s physical form, a thought arose in his mind:
"This is the image of Śākyamuni Buddha with its marks and signs."
Continuing with the recollection of the Buddha’s merits:
"The Buddha is the Omniscient One, endowed with great kindness and great compassion, the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and other such merits."
Having thought this, his heart burned and his hair stood on end; he immediately offered the flower to the Buddha.
Having offered it to the Buddha, he thought:
"Although I have heard the Buddha say that offering even a single flower will surely result in a great reward, I do not know the limits or the measure of such merit."
He immediately went out and saw a monk who exhorted others to practice;
he asked him, "If one scatters a single flower upon the Buddha, how much merit and virtue is obtained?
He replied:
"I have grown weary of the suffering of the world; I have merely renounced the five desires, left the household life, and received the precepts.
As for such profound matters as these, I am unable to know them; I must ask those who are wise and learned in the recitation of the scriptures!"
He immediately went to ask a man who recited the scriptures, who replied:
"I am like a painter; according to what I have heard and seen, I possess no divine eye or supernormal powers, and thus cannot know or see the retributions of good and evil."
He immediately pointed out a practitioner of seated meditation (dhyāna-yogin) who could be approached and asked:
"The senior practitioner of seated meditation is a ṣaḍabhijña arhat; he will surely know this matter!
He then went at once to inquire about the merit of mindfulness of the Buddha (buddhānusmṛti).
“With my heart burning and my hair standing on end, I scattered a single flower upon the Buddha; how much merit and virtue have I gained?
The Arhat then contemplated this for him:

“After casting off this body, he will successively receive merit and virtue among devas and humans. From one lifetime through ten million billion lifetimes, from one great kalpa up to eighty thousand great kalpas, his merit will still not be exhausted. Beyond this point, it can no longer be known.”
The Arhat, considering himself highly esteemed by the assembly and wondering how he could be unaware of even a single fruit or flower as karmic retribution,
said to the man:
"Wait a moment."
Having spoken thus, he dispatched a transformation body to the Tuṣita Heaven to visit Maitreya.
He reported in full what the worthy one had said, representing him to Maitreya:
"What kind of karmic fruit has been obtained?"
Maitreya replied:
"I cannot know it!
Even bodhisattvas who are in their last birth before buddhahood, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, would still be unable to know it; how much less so could I alone?"
Why is this? The Buddha possesses immeasurable merit; he is a most excellent field of blessings, wherein various fruits of retribution are inexhaustible.
Only when I have attained Buddhahood in the future shall I be able to know them!
The Sūtra on the Miscellaneous Collection Spoken by the Buddha.
